# What is reproducibility?

## Reproducibility is not binary

Reproducibility is best seen as a continuum within a multidimensional space:

- **repeatability**: can others obtain the same results given access to the same data?
- **transparency**: are explanations good enough to be understood by others?
- **accessibility**: can others find and download the exact data and code used?
- **compatibility**: can they run the code on a different computer/OS today?
- **sustainability**: will the code still run in X years after package updates?
- **generalisability**: can the code be applied to a new, similar dataset?

. . .

\vspace{1cm}

**NB:**

- names are my own (many synonymous exist)
- improving any dimension takes intentional time/effort and introduce trade-offs (e.g. improving generalisability decreases clarity)
- in this very short introduction, I focus on **repeatability**


# Why making workflows reproducible?

## Increasing reproducibility benefits people

Given that reproducibility comes at a cost, the main question to answer is:

### who shall benefit from the effort of making your code reproducible?

. . .

- yourself

  - [x] yourself right now
  - [ ] yourself in the near future (e.g. writing the paper)
  - [ ] yourself in the distant future (e.g. analysing similar data)

. . .

\vspace{0.5em}
- your immediate circle

  - [ ] your supervisor / PI
  - [ ] your colleagues and collaborators
  - [ ] potential reviewers, auditors, or evaluators

. . .

\vspace{0.5em}
- the wider community

  - [ ] those interested in your data
  - [ ] those interested in your research question
  - [ ] those interested in your methodology

. . .

**NB:** many answers can simultaneously apply


## Universal benefits of repeatable code

In comparison to just producing results on the fly (i.e. taken from the R console), writing repeatable scripts/documents provides the following benefits:

- it prevents coding mistakes
- exactly what you did is tracked^[a repeatable code tracks what code does but not how the code changed over time;\
 the latter can instead can be done using a version control system, such as git/GitHub]
- updating the results after updating the data is easy


# How to make workflows repeatable?

## Various approach can be used to improve repeatability of R-based workflows

```{r}
#| echo: false
df <- data.frame(Tool = c("R script", "R package*", "sweave", "rmarkdown/quarto"),
                 "Literate programming**" = c("no", "yes", "yes", "yes"),
                 Setup = c("simple", "difficult", "medium", "simple"),
                 "Learning curve" = c("low", "high", "high", "low/mid"),
                 check.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(df, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lccc") |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 10)
```
\*i.e a specific R package which main goal is to reproduce the results of a workflow

\**mixing prose and code

. . .

**Conclusion:**

- rmarkdown/quarto improves repeatability at low cost
- syntax errors in rmarkdown/quarto can be frustrating, but LLMs are exceptionally efficient at debugging these specific issues
- quarto can do the same & more than rmarkdown, so I will focus on that


# A quick introduction to quarto

## What is quarto?

It is defined as an "open-source scientific and technical publishing system"

```{r}
#| out-height: "10cm"
#| fig-align: center
knitr::include_graphics("figures/rstudio-qmd-how-it-works.png", dpi = NA) # dpi = NA fix aspect ratio issue
```

- the R package {knitr} converts quarto files into the markdown format
- the software pandoc converts markdown files into various output formats


## Key structure

1. a header defining the general properties of the document, in YAML format
2. text in markdown, html, or LaTeX
3. chunks of computer code


## The header

### Minimal example

```
---
title: "Some title"
format: html
---
```

## The header

The header is a particularly fragile component

- spacing matters
- copy/pasting headers across documents usually leads to unattended changes
- much of the content must be tailored to the selected output format


## The text

This is the easy part

- write plain text and use `#`, `##`, `###` to define a hierarchy of sections\
  (if the hierarchy is messed up it can be because a chunk is located at the highest level of the hierarchy)
- use `*text*`, `**text**`, `***text***`, to create *text*, **text** & ***text***, respectively
- use `[link_text](weblink)` to create hyperlinks


## Chunks of R code

\begingroup\footnotesize
````markdown
`r ''````{r}
#| option1: argument for option1
...
#| optionN: argument for optionN
some R code
```
````
\endgroup

### Example

\begingroup\footnotesize
````markdown
`r ''````{r}
#| label: illustrating filter
#| echo: true
#| message: true
species_count |> filter(year == 2025)
```
````
\endgroup

. . .


**Pro tips:**

- defining labels using `#| label: some label` helps to identify where issues arise
- render the document frequently to discover mistakes soon after they are introduced

# Beyond repeatability

## How to improve other aspects of reproducibility

::: {.incremental}
- **transparency**: document *why* you do things and not just *how* you do things
- **accessibility**: host your data and code on platforms such as GitHub, Zenodo, ...
- **compatibility**: make sure to try your code on other computers
- **sustainability**: minimize external dependencies; at minima document package version using `sessionInfo()`, or better use systems such as {renv} which save and load specific versions of R packages; for longer sustainability learn how to build containers (e.g. docker)
- **generalisability**: design functions, do not hardcode parameters, do not use indices
:::

. . .

\vspace{1cm}

**NB:**

- many of these improvements can be achieved at minimal costs
- remember that repeatability is a continuum (e.g. the more generalizable the code one wants, the more effort one must put into creating the code)
